Understanding the Interplay between Parametric and Contextual Knowledge for Large Language Models

Sitao Cheng, Liangming Pan, Xunjian Yin, Xinyi Wang, William Yang Wang

Paper ↗Code ↗

Providing relevant context can make a model less willing to use facts it already knows; EchoQA tests when internal knowledge and external information work together or interfere.

01 / The research question

Knowing both facts is not the same as combining them

A retrieval system often supplies only the missing part of an answer. The model must connect that new evidence with knowledge already available in its parameters. This setting is different from asking whether to trust a retrieved passage that contradicts memory. Both sources can be correct and individually useful, while neither is sufficient alone. EchoQA studies this complementary case alongside conflicting and irrelevant context.

The recorded case makes a subtle distinction visible. Without context, a model can select the right answer through a biologically plausible shortcut while misidentifying the entity. With complementary context, it may resolve that entity correctly yet fail to recall the next fact. Neither the final answer alone nor the availability of relevant context fully describes whether composition succeeded.

03 / Inside the method

Separate knowledge availability from knowledge use

The benchmark first checks the underlying parametric fact with a direct question for each model. It then constructs cases where external context supplies a different necessary fact. This filtering makes a failure more informative: the prerequisite was elicitable before the composition task. It also means models can be evaluated on different retained examples, so cross-model comparisons are not always comparisons over an identical set of questions.

The prompting conditions probe progressively stronger assistance. The neutral instruction already asks the model to combine its knowledge with the context. Other instructions explicitly emphasize internal knowledge or ask the model to recall it before reasoning. A golden-context condition places all needed facts in the prompt. That last comparison asks whether bringing both premises into the same source is easier than connecting memory to context.

Different relationships require different interpretations. In a conflicting case, following memory may preserve a known true fact against fabricated context. In a complementary case, the model must use both. With irrelevant context, it should avoid treating a distractor as a reason to abandon an answer it previously knew. A single preference for memory or retrieval cannot solve all three.

  1. 01

    Establish known facts

    First test each model without context and retain knowledge it can answer, creating a model-specific starting point.

  2. 02

    Control the relationship

    Construct supportive, complementary, conflicting, and irrelevant contexts across scientific, factual, and commonsense knowledge.

  3. 03

    Measure information use

    Compare answer accuracy and uncertainty under different instructions, including prompts encouraging the model to use its own knowledge.

04 / Reading the evidence

Abstention can reveal a missing connection

  • 62.72%

    Answers marked unknown

    Llama 3.1-70B's unknown-answer rate rises from 23.89% without context to 62.72% with complementary scientific context under neutral instructions.

  • 23.88%

    After instruction changes

    Encouraging the same model to trust its own knowledge lowers that uncertainty, although improved prompting does not eliminate the integration problem.

For LLaMA3.1-70B on complementary ALCUNA examples, the unknown-answer rate is 62.72% with the neutral instruction, 23.88% when explicitly encouraged to trust its knowledge, and 0.08% with golden context. These are abstention rates, not accuracy scores. The near-removal of abstention when both facts are written out is evidence that source integration matters; it does not establish that every resulting answer is correct.

The paper also examines 200 selected failure cases and finds frequent reasoning confined to the supplied context or answer choices. This is diagnostic evidence about those failures, not an estimate of behavior on all questions. Explicit prompting helps, yet requires guidance about source sufficiency that an application may not possess. The study motivates evaluating source composition directly rather than assuming a strong standalone fact score guarantees reliable retrieval-augmented reasoning.

Research summary

Large language models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of knowledge during pre-training (parametric knowledge, or PK) and can further be enhanced by incorporating contextual knowledge (CK). Can LLMs effectively integrate their internal PK with external CK to solve complex problems? In this paper, we investigate the dynamic interaction between PK and CK, categorizing their relationships into four types: Supportive, Complementary, Conflicting, and Irrelevant. To support this investigation, we introduce EchoQA, a benchmark spanning scientific, factual, and commonsense knowledge. Our results show that LLMs tend to suppress their PK when contextual information is available, even when it is complementary or irrelevant. While tailored instructions can encourage LLMs to rely more on their PK, they still struggle to fully leverage it. These findings reveal a key vulnerability in LLMs, raising concerns about their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks.
